paper_title: Embodied Turing Machines: Stateful Code for Robot Recursive Self-Improvement

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Most robot policies keep a model in the control loop: a VLA maps observations to actions, and an Agent Harness, such as Agent-as-Policy or Harness VLA queries a VLM for decision making at run time. We propose a different view: the embodied world is an Embodied Turing Machine, whose tape is the robot and environment state and rules are the policy. If this state can be represented accurately, the decision making can be written entirely in code. We therefore propose Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP): code measures and tracks the robot, environment, and task state from camera images and proprioception, and makes every decision from it. The same code applies across episodes, and different tasks share one library without a VLM or VLA in the loop. Compared with VLAs and Agent Harnesses, we analyze three advantages of COAP: (i) Explicit State: the state can be stored in code; (ii) Execution: code makes decision making controllable, recovers from failures flexibly, and runs fast and cheaply online; (iii) Extensibility: new tasks reuse, inherit, or extend the shared library, so capabilities can accumulate over tasks. These advantages make COAP a suitable medium for recursive self-improvement (RSI): coding agents develop the library in a closed loop, and each change is explicit and controllable. On RoboDojo's 42 bimanual tasks, the resulting library reaches a success rate of 70.24% without a model at test time. The upper bound of COAP lies in how accurately the state is represented for decision making and how robust the code logic is. We thus propose COAP as a new paradigm for embodied tasks; since it applies across episodes, it can also serve as an efficient data engine for VLAs and Agent Harnesses.

Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP). We view the embodied world as an Embodied Turing Machine whose tape is the state of the robot and its environment (top middle). If this state is represented accurately and the code is robust enough, no agent is needed in the control loop (top right). COAP is shared library: different tasks use the same library, and within task the code runs across episodes. The policy is therefore code only and reaches 70.24% success rate on RoboDojo.

The same code applies across episodes, and different tasks share one library without VLM or VLA in the loop. Technical Report. * Equal contribution. 1 Compared with VLAs and Agent Harnesses, we analyze three advantages of COAP: (i) Explicit State: the state can be stored in code; (ii) Execution: code makes decision making controllable, recovers from failures flexibly, and runs fast and cheaply online; (iii) Extensibility: new tasks reuse, inherit, or extend the shared library, so capabilities can accumulate over tasks. These advantages make COAP suitable medium for recursive self-improvement (RSI): coding agents develop the library in closed loop, and each change is explicit and controllable. On RoboDojos 42 bimanual tasks, the resulting library reaches success rate of 70.24% without model at test time. The upper bound of COAP lies in how accurately the state is represented for decision making and how robust the code logic is. We thus propose COAP as new paradigm for embodied tasks; since it applies across episodes, it can also serve as an efficient data engine for VLAs and Agent Harnesses. 1. Introduction It is possible to invent single machine which can be used to compute any computable sequence. Alan Turing [60] Turing machine comprises tape that stores symbols and set of fixed rules that read from and write to the tape [60]. With the rules fixed and only the tape varying, the same rules can process arbitrary inputs. The same abstraction applies to the physical world, where the world state is analogous to the tape. robot reads this tape through perception and writes to it through action, and its policy plays the role of the rules. We therefore model robot and its environment as an Embodied Turing Machine, whose tape holds two kinds of state: the environment state (e.g., object poses and their spatial relations) and the robot state (e.g., arm pose and reachable poses). Both kinds of state are accurately observable. The robot state is available directly through proprioception, and object poses can be recovered from RGB images using measured object geometry. policy that acts on this state gains two advantages. First, more accurate state enables more precise action. Second, when objects are rearranged (like different episodes in task), only the tape changes, and the same rules (policy) still apply. policy can map state to action in three ways, which differ in how explicit this mapping is. (i) Vision-language-action models (VLAs). VLA takes observations, such as camera images, as input and learns the mapping to action, which remains implicit in its weights [4, 19]. (ii) Agent harnesses. The vision-language model (VLM) either controls the robot directly, as in Agent-as-Policy, or directs VLA, as in Harness VLA [9, 55]. The harness makes part of the process explicit, such as textual memory, but the VLM and VLA remain black boxes, so we may still neither fully inspect nor control how an action is derived. (iii) Code-Only-as-Policy (ours). In contrast, code is white box that implements the Embodied Turing Machine directly: the state, such as object poses, is stored in code variables, where it remains accurate, persistent, and explicit; the rules are written as code logic that computes each action from this state. With both the state and the rules explicit, no model is required at runtime: the code is frozen and serves as the sole policy during execution. Code thus becomes universal interface to the physical world: single code program takes over the roles of the VLAs, the prompts and skills of Agent-as-Policy, and the memory of Harness VLA. 2 Figure 2. Comparison of code-based robot policies. In prior work, model writes code-as-policy online, turn by turn, as the robot runs (left), or one program takes its state from learned model or the simulator oracle (middle). Our COAP reuses code across episodes and measures the state by code (right). Existing code-based policies either (i) ask model to write new code-as-policy online in each episode of task [21, 59, 62], or (ii) take the state from model or the simulators oracle [11, 39] (Figure 2). COAP instead measures the state with its own code and builds shared code library for perception and execution. Different tasks run the same library code, and only small part of the logic is task-specific: 83% of the code that new task runs comes from the library. Nor is the code written for particular episode: one program runs on every episode of task. Because the task is fixed, code that is robust enough needs no VLM or VLA in the loop; if it still needs one, the code is not yet robust enough to run reliably across episodes. Code-Only-as-Policy has three advantages (4.3). (i) Explicit State: the state is stored in code variables, and every decision is made from them (4.3.1). (ii) Execution: the code gives fine-grained control over the state and actions, recovers from failures flexibly by backtracking and re-attempting, and runs fast and cheaply online (4.3.2). (iii) Extensibility: new task reuses, inherits, or extends the shared library, so the code evolves quickly and capabilities accumulate (4.3.3). Hence, COAP is suitable medium for stable recursive self-improvement (RSI) (4.4). Since the code is not specific to any episode, one policy runs on different episodes and can generate successful trajectories efficiently for VLAs and Agent Harnesses (5.5). We evaluate COAP on RoboDojos 42 bimanual tasks [7]. coding agent (Opus 5.5 Max) develop the code library in closed RSI loop that we design: under fixed rules, such as no hack for single episodes and no oracle state at test time, the coding agent summarizes, writes, and debugs the code without human in the loop. The development does not involve test set of benchmark. The resulting COAP policy reaches 70.24% success rate, 38.9% above the state-ofthe-art method. The upper bound of COAP can be pushed further if the state representation gets more accurate and code logic grows more robust. The weakness of COAP mainly lies in its generalization capabilities since it needs small amount of task-specific code logic. However, Agent-as-Policy and Harness VLA also involve task-level memories, and some even rely on episode-level logic. In this work, our aim is to explore the upper bound of Code-Only-as-Policy for the community. Moreover, COAP also generates successful trajectories stably and efficiently, which can benefit the development of VLAs and Agent Harnesses (5.5). Our contributions are: (i) Code-Only-as-Policy. We view the embodied world as Turing machine in which the robot and environment state can be represented explicitly. The same code applies to different episodes, and different tasks use shared library developed offline by coding agent. (ii) Advantages of Code-Only-as-Policy. We analyze three advantages of code over VLAs and Agent Harnesses: Explicit State, Execution, and Extensibility. We explore code-only as new paradigm for embodied task: when the code is robust enough and applies across episodes, no VLM or VLA is required during runtime. (iii) Code as the medium of RSI. Code iterates efficiently, and each change is controllable. CodeOnly-as-Policy can also serve as an efficient data engine to produce beneficial trajectories as new training data for VLAs, Agent-as-Policy, etc. 2. Related Work Existing robot policies built with foundation models differ in where they keep the state and how they choose each action from it  (Table 1)  : VLA encodes the state implicitly in its weights, and an Agent Harness (Agent-as-Policy or Harness VLA) stores it as text in models context. Vision-language-action models. RT-2, OpenVLA, 𝜋0, and 𝜋0.5 learn language-conditioned visuomotor policies end to end [4, 5, 19, 36], and recent foundation models scale data and training further [18, 48]. VLA cannot be inspected or edited directly, so each improvement requires new data and new training run, and LIBERO-PRO shows that benchmark success can reflect memorized training configurations [58]. In comparison, we keep the state in code variables, so we can backtrack from failure to the variable that caused it and fix the code logic that derived it. Each accepted fix is merged into the code without breaking existing logic, so improvements accumulate, while training VLA on new task can degrade its performance on earlier tasks [61]. VLM (System-2) for robot control. ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions [53], and Toolformer teaches model to call tools [38]. In robotics, SayCan grounds language-model plans in learned affordances [1], and Inner Monologue feeds environment feedback back to the planner [16]. Recent harnesses let VLM agent call analytic or learned primitives [9, 55], and GPT-6 Astra [34] has been evaluated directly as an embodied policy [43, 56]. In these systems, the model is queried repeatedly during execution to output actions, so there is randomness at each call, even if the prompt is the same. Moreover, every episode is of high cost due to extensive model calls [35]. In our approach, models are used only offline: coding agents write the code, and the robot runs it without model during online execution. The code computes each action from the state through explicit rules, so the robots behaviour is reproducible, and each decision is cheap because model calls are not required. Code-as-Policy. Code-based policies differ in when the program is written and in the source of the state used (Figure 2). Code-as-Policies and ProgPrompt prompt language model to write code that calls perception and control APIs [21, 41], and VoxPoser writes code that composes spatial value maps [17]. Later works add execution feedback, repeated generation, and skill discovery [12, 26, 30]. PyRUA-Lean has model write code cell by cell as each episode runs [59], and Skill2Real has model compose new program from frozen skill memories at each decision stage [62]. In these systems, model writes the program at runtime, and the state is provided by learned perception models: object detectors in Code as Policies, and SAM in PyRUA-Lean and Skill2Real. In RHO and EmbodiedSWE, coding agents write one program offline, but its state still comes from outside the code: RHO likewise obtains it from SAM and Molmo [6, 11], and the solvers of EmbodiedSWE read the simulators oracle values [39]. In contrast, our code tracks the state itself, so the state is programmable: when measurement is wrong, coding agents fix the measurement code, and the state becomes more accurate over time. Code as an interface for agents. Outside robotics, code has become the medium through which agents act and improve. CodeAct uses executable code as the action space of an agent [46], and exposing tools as code API lets model compose them with fewer tokens [2, 44]. Voyager grows library of code skills through interaction [45], and software agents solve long-horizon repository tasks through tests and diffs [33, 50]. In these settings, the environment provides the state explicitly, as files, test results, or game API values. robot, in contrast, must measure its state from sensors, and our code performs this measurement itself. In robotics, RoboRSI runs RSI as loop of manager, planner, engineer, and reviewer agents with no-regression gate, but VLM still makes the decisions during execution [32]. change that passes the gate only steers this black box, whose uncertainty and errors cannot be fully controlled, so the tested behaviour may not be the behaviour at runtime. Our policy is code with explicit state, so the tested behaviour is the behaviour at runtime, and coding agents can improve it the way software engineers improve program: every change is tested offline, and only changes that improve results without regressions on other tasks are merged. Benchmarks. LIBERO measures knowledge transfer in lifelong robot learning [24], RoboTwin 2.0 generates domain-randomized bimanual tasks [8], and RoboCasa365 scales household simulation [31]. RoboDojo spans memory, precision, open instructions, generalization, and long-horizon manipulation in one protocol [7]. Its memory and precision tasks directly test how well policy retains and measures state, and the shared protocol lets us compare VLAs, world models, agents, and code on the same 42 tasks. 3. Embodied Turing Machine: Code-Only-as-Policy Code-Only-as-Policy implements the Embodied Turing Machine (1) as shared code library, in which code variables hold the state and the source code constitutes the rules. Beyond storing the state, the perception code measures the environment from camera images, and the code 5 Figure 3. Code-Only-as-Policy. Development (left): coding agents improve the code offline in loop. They run the current code 𝜃𝑘 on development layouts, read the state, and run alternative diffs on branches in parallel. Shared library (middle): task programs call the library from the shared code. Execution (right): at runtime the robot runs one fixed task program across episode, and an agent and VLA are not required. updates these measurements as the robot acts. The code is frozen at runtime and improved offline by coding agents (Figure 3). The development does not involve test set of benchmark. 3.1. Reading and writing the state At step 𝑡, RoboDojo provides an observation 𝑜𝑡 consisting of an instruction, three RGB images (head and two wrists), joint angles, end-effector poses, and the gripper command echo [7]. The code maintains an explicit state 𝑥𝑡 with three parts, each of which has the same form in every task. (i) The environment state records the pose, size, and category of each object and the spatial relations between objects, such as one object resting on another; each record also stores the error, source, and time of its measurement. (ii) The robot state records the joint angles, end-effector pose, and gripper opening of each arm, together with the poses each arm can reach. These two parts represent the tape of the Embodied Turing Machine. (iii) The task state records the current stage, the arm assigned to each object, retry counts, and the information the task must retain, such as the color under each cup. It is not part of the tape and plays the role of the internal state of Turing machine. Each part is updated from different source. The robot state is obtained from proprioception at every step. The environment state is measured by perception layer library. The task code updates the task state during execution. The source code 𝜃 constitutes the rules. In each frame, the robots mesh is projected into the image using the measured joint angles, and the pixels it covers are masked out. (2) perception for each kind of object then places the known 3D shape of the candidate near 𝑝, searches over its position and yaw, and keeps the fit with the largest overlap with the observed region. The camera models, robot meshes, object shapes, and table height used in these steps are published with the benchmark and do not change between episodes, so they are constants in the code, part of the rules 𝜃. Each matched measurement yields an object record with category, position, yaw, size, and confidence. Records persist in an episode-level WorldState: an object occluded by the arm keeps its last measured pose. Tasks that require millimetre accuracy re-measure the object with wrist camera before the final approach. 3.3. Sharing one library across tasks that read the same state Two design choices make the library reusable across tasks. (i) Every task operates on state of the same form (3.1), so module written for one task can be reused by other tasks. (ii) The code is layered, with dependencies pointing downward (Figure 3, middle): task programs call object-specific code, which calls manipulation code such as grasp, pick, place, push, and pour, which in turn calls perception and motion code. Task code specifies what to do: the order of subgoals, task-specific decisions, and recovery conditions. The lower layers determine how. For example, single transfer call expands into grasp-candidate generation, inverse-kinematics and collision filtering, pre-grasp re-measurement, approach, closure, short lift with hold check, carry, placement, release, and final verification, each of which returns an outcome with measured evidence. As result, 83% of the lines are shared across tasks (4.3.3). new task extends the library in one of three ways (Code Example 2). It can compose existing modules, such as transfer. It can inherit an existing task and override single decision: task that sorts objects into the baskets named in its instruction reuses the entire flow of an existing sorting task and replaces only the rule that assigns objects to baskets. Or it can add default-off parameter to shared function: lift_dir allows grasped object to be lifted diagonally, which one task requires near basket wall, while the default preserves the existing vertical lift. Improving the code by backtracking failures to the state Because the code records its state at every step of an episode, coding agents can improve the code offline from these records. Improvement proceeds in rounds and is carried out by Claude Opus 5.5 coding agents, which wrote all code in the library and in every task, ran the tests and evaluations, and debugged their own code autonomously. Let 𝜃𝑘 be the accepted code after round 𝑘. Each agent works in its own git worktree, inspects the recorded state of failed development runs to locate the variable or rule at fault, and proposes diff Δ. The resulting branches form search frontier of runnable code: C𝑘 = {𝜃𝑘 + Δ𝑘,1, . . . , 𝜃𝑘 + Δ𝑘,𝑚}. (4) Because each branch is complete, runnable code, branches can be evaluated concurrently under identical conditions. Before simulation, each branch passes two CPU checks: the task code is executed against numeric scene to confirm that every stage reaches its target state, and the robot and object meshes are checked for inverse-kinematics solutions and collisions at every waypoint. Branches that pass are evaluated on the validation episodes (4.1) in parallel. Debugging and selection use separate data. Agents debug on development set they define themselves, where they watch videos and compare the measured state against simulator ground truth; selection compares success counts on the validation split. Let 𝐽𝑞(𝜃; 𝑉𝑞) be the success count of task 𝑞 on these layouts and 𝜖𝑞 margin above rerun noise. branch is accepted if 𝐽𝑞(𝜃𝑘 + Δ; 𝑉𝑞) 𝐽𝑞(𝜃𝑘; 𝑉𝑞) + 𝜖𝑞, (5) in which case it becomes 𝜃𝑘+1 and the base of all subsequent branches. Otherwise, the current code remains deployed and the diff is not merged. The compatibility condition (Equation 3) protects the tasks that diff does not target, and the acceptance rule (Equation 5) ensures that the targeted task improves, so each accepted step is non-decreasing and improvements accumulate. 4. Experiments This section answers three questions: (1) How well does Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP) perform on hard benchmark (4.14.2)? (2) What does COAP offer that VLA or an Agent Harness lacks (4.3)? (3) Why does COAP suit RSI (4.4)? 4.1. Setup Benchmark and protocol. Each task is evaluated with three seeds of 50 layouts each. All reported numbers are produced by the official evaluation client, judges, and summary script. Inputs. Main results Table 2 compares Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP) with the leaderboard. COAP achieves success rate of 70.24%, 38.9 percentage points above the current state-of-the-art method (31.38%), and more than 40 points above the strongest World Action Model (29.64%), and the strongest VLA (27.96%). COAP also has the highest success rate in each of the five dimensions. The margins are largest on Memory (89.9%, 39.6 points above the best baseline) and Precision (75.1%, 41.6 points), the two dimensions in which the next action depends on stored value or precise measurement. COAP reaches 65.7% on Generalization (77.3% on standard and 54.1% on 10 randomized layouts) and 64.1% on Open. Its margin is smallest on Long-Horizon tasks. 4.3. Advantages of Code-Only-as-Policy We compare Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP) with VLA and an Agent Harness on three advantages, summarized in Figure 4: Explicit State (4.3.1), Execution (4.3.2), and Extensibility (4.3.3). For each baseline, we use the strongest leaderboard entry of its category  (Table 2)  . Where the benchmark provides no measurement, we use numbers reported in prior work [4, 19, 36, 61]. Figure 4. Three advantages of COAP, each with three properties. 4.3.1. Explicit State Finding 1. Code-Only-as-Policy stores the robot, environment, and task state as explicit variables and computes actions from them. In comparison, an Agent Harness keeps the state in text memory and its model context, and VLA keeps it implicitly in its weights. A1 Inspectable. Code-Only-as-Policy is white box. What the program perceives about the robot and the environment becomes explicit state in code: variables, data structures, and the Figure 5. Explicit State. COAP keeps five categories of state as variables (left), remembers states and values (middle), and succeeds more often with more accurate measurements (right). parameters of functions. As shown in Figure 5 (left), the state has five categories: robot, object, environment, relation, and task. The coding agent can therefore write the decisions in advance as code over these values, so no agent is needed during online execution. In comparison, in VLA, both the state and the reasoning are implicit in the weights. An Agent Harness keeps the task memory, but its decisions still come from model inference: an agent or VLA still does the reasoning, so some states stay hidden in this model-in-the-loop system, which cannot be fully inspected (even the same memory can lead to different actions at different calls). A2 Persistent. COAP stores each measured value in variable of the program, and the value persists throughout the execution. For example, when static object is covered, its position and pose are still tracked in code, as shown in Figure 5 (middle). Decisions that depend on memory, such as following specific order, are also written explicitly in code. In comparison, VLA sees only its recent frames, and an Agent Harness keeps what it has seen only in its model context or text memory. Memory-related tasks can therefore be solved easily by code, since the state is tracked and stored persistently in the program: on the Memory tasks of RoboDojo, COAP reaches 90%, against 47% for the Agent Harness and 33% for the VLA. A3 Accurate. COAP acts on measured quantities, because the measurements can be estimated offline without accessing the simulators oracle values. The cameras, the robots 3D meshes, and the sizes and appearance of the objects are estimated before deployment, so at test time the program only locates each object, its position, size, and pose, and sets the grasp width and the clearance from them. During development, the oracle values help improve the perception functions, so the success rate on measured state can approach that on oracle values: as shown in Figure 5 (right), the same program succeeds in 63% of episodes on measured state and in 83% on oracle state, and each measurement that is fixed narrows this gap. In comparison, VLA and an Agent Harness act mainly on image pixels and never make measurements explicit. COAP therefore has higher upper bound on tasks that need precision: on the Precision tasks of RoboDojo, it reaches 75%, against 33% for the Agent Harness and 27% for the VLA. Figure 6. Execution. Backtracking keeps failures from compounding over long tasks (left, middle), and code runs on CPU with small fraction of models compute (right; COAPs compute as share of each models, from reported model sizes). 12 4.3.2. Execution Finding 2. Code-Only-as-Policy controls the state and the decision making. Because the state is tracked, failures can be recovered by backtracking and re-attempting through the robust code design. Online execution is efficient and cheap since it is model-free. B1 Controllable. COAP has no model in the online execution, so code controls the state, its variables, and the decision making. For example, when bowl held by its rim slipped during fast carries, one line of code limited the carry speed of rim grasps, and the bowl no longer dropped. In comparison, VLA, or model in the loop of an Agent Harness, is black box: some of its uncertainty and errors cannot be fully controlled and accumulate over the execution. More training trajectories for VLA, or more text memory for an Agent Harness, still leave its decisions uncertain. B2 Recoverable. Because the state is tracked and controlled, the program knows where the task stands after each step, so it can backtrack and re-attempt. As shown in Figure 6 (middle, bottom), when an initial grasp fails, the program backtracks, measures the object again, and re-attempts with new grasp method, such as new grasp angle. In episodes where something went wrong, the program noticed the problem itself in 76% and re-attempted with new method in 34% (Figure 6, middle). Recovery matters more as tasks grow longer, since without it one failed step ends the task (Figure 6, left). In comparison, VLA has no tracked state to return to. B3 Efficient. COAP uses model only offline, when the coding agent writes the code, and the code is shared by every episode of task. control step takes median of 0.3 ms on CPU, and an episode uses 0.82.4% of the compute of VLA and less than 0.1% of that of an Agent Harness (Figure 6, right). In comparison, an Agent Harness, especially GPT-as-policy, is much slower and more expensive, and it reasons anew in every episode instead of sharing its decisions across the episodes of task. 4.3.3. Extensibility Finding 3. Code-Only-as-Policy builds every new task on shared library by reusing, inheriting, or extending its code. Each new task is therefore fast to develop, and capabilities accumulate without harming the performance on old tasks. C1 Reusable. new task reuses, inherits, or extends the shared library, so its own code holds only task-specific logic, such as check or picking order. As shown in Figure 7 (left), 83% of the code that new tasks run comes from the library. The library can be shared because its functions are abstracted step by step at sensible level (Figure 8). For example, grasping is not written for each object but by grasp method, such as from the top, by the rim, or by the handle, so new object can use an existing method. In comparison, VLA needs fine-tuning for new tasks. The memory of an Agent Harness is task-specific and cannot be shared, and its execution is specific to each episode, so it cannot be shared either. C2 Fast to evolve. Since the library is shared, new task can reuse, inherit, or extend the existing library, so COAP evolves easily to new tasks. Figure 7 (middle) shows development on new tasks from scratch, on tasks that had no program when the library was frozen. COAP reached an average success of 47% within 15 hours, without data or training. Its curve rises steeply, because the library becomes more robust as it grows, and every task benefits from it. The baseline lines are schematic. VLA needs new demonstrations and retraining; OpenVLA, 13 Figure 7. Extensibility. New tasks run mostly library code (left), are developed from scratch within hours without data or training (middle; baseline lines are schematic), and add to what the policy can do (right, schematic). Figure 8. Code structure. (a) The layers of the library. (b) Functions are abstracted at sensible level: grasping is written by grasp method, not by object. (c) simplified task program; each call is colored by its layer. for example, reports 515 hours of fine-tuning per task on 8 A100 GPUs [19]. On the same tasks, the strongest VLA reaches 4.7% after training on demonstrations. An Agent Harness improves roughly linearly and much more slowly: most of its memory is task-specific, and only small part, such as general insights, carries over between tasks. C3 Cumulative. The library is designed to be refactorable: new task adds functions that inherit from existing ones, or options that are off by default, instead of changing the logic of earlier tasks. Earlier tasks therefore keep running unchanged code, and capabilities can be added without making old tasks worse. As the code becomes more robust, each new task becomes simpler to add, so the capabilities of COAP grow exponentially (Figure 7, right; schematic). In comparison, an Agent Harness builds task-specific memory by running each task and reuses little of it, so its capabilities grow linearly. VLA must be retrained for new tasks, and the effect on old tasks cannot be controlled: after sequential fine-tuning of 𝜋0.5 on five real-world tasks, its average score drops from 86.9 to 31.4 [61]. 14 Figure 9. Why Code-Only-as-Policy is suitable medium for RSI. Each row is an attribute important for RSI, which comes from an advantage in Section 4.3 (check: yes; half circle: partly; cross: no). Figure 10. Parallel branching over the variants of one decision. (a) Development as BFS: eight grasps of mug run at once, and the best code logic is chosen (decisions 2 and 3 are schematic). (b) Of 36 branches, each measured against its parent, few help. (c) With more branches, an accepted change is more likely and larger. (d) With more branches, an accepted change comes sooner in wall-clock time, for more GPU time. 4.4. Why Code-Only-as-Policy Suits RSI Finding 4. Code-Only-as-Policy suits RSI because of its three advantages: Explicit State, Execution, and Extensibility. Because execution is controllable, development is also efficient. The variants of decision can be developed in parallel, like Breadth-First Search (BFS). What are important attributes for RSI? Figure 9 lists four attributes that we think are important for RSI, and COAP is better interface for all four. RSI repeats one loop: find failure, change the policy, and keep the change if it helps. Efficient: fast evolving through parallel branching. Development can be organized as BFS 15 over decisions. Each node is decision, such as how to grasp mug, and its branches are different ways to make it, such as grasping the mug by its rim, its handle, or its body. Because every variant is complete program that needs no training, the branches are developed in parallel on the same layouts, and the best code logic is chosen before the search moves on to the next decision (Figure 10). In comparison, each branch of VLA would be training run, and an Agent Harness calls large model in every rollout. As shown in Figure 10, single change rarely helps, but with more branches, better change is found more often, its gain is larger, and it comes sooner in wall-clock time, at the cost of more GPU time. Our development records show the same trend: decisions tried with two or more variants found an accepted change in four of five cases. 5. Discussion This section discusses what the state of Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP) should contain (5.1), where COAP still fails (5.2), what sets its upper bound (5.3), its limitations (5.4), and how it can serve as data engine (5.5). 5.1. What Should the State Contain? The state is the tape of the Turing machine (3), and its five categories are shown in Figure 5 (left). The robot state describes the robot itself: its joint angles, hand poses, gripper openings, and what each hand holds. The environment state describes the position, size, and class of each object, the table, and the objects spatial relations, such as which object stands on which. The task state records the task progress, such as the objects picked so far and the current subgoal. All values are in physical units and are stored in the program. 5.2. Error Analysis of COAP Finding 5. COAP still fails in some episodes. The current coding ability has limits, and the offline RSI loop needs further optimization so that coding agents write better code. The failures fall into two groups: limits of state measurement and limits of the code logic. We assigned failed episodes of the runs in Table 2 to the class of the smallest change that would have prevented them. Figure 11 shows the share of each class and one example of each. Perception error. The input is RGB only, and recognition is not always accurate, so wrong value can enter the state. In Figure 11a, dartboard in randomized scene is recognized as the headset. Such errors may be more severe in real scenes, but better estimation and tools can help. Contact error. In principle, the more clearly the state is represented, the higher the upper bound of the code. For contact, especially with deformable objects, the current representation of the state is coarse and unclear, so the program cannot always tell how an object is held. Such contact is inherently hard to represent, but it is still limit of the state representation. In Figure 11b, the jaws close on shirts hem, and the soft cloth slips out. Incomplete logic. The code logic is not robust enough, for example because retry is missing. In Figure 11c, the push function stops after one push, although its own check finds cube still turned. Within the limited development time, the code was not made fully robust. 16 Poor code design. function works in the cases it was written for but does not generalize, for example because of hard-coded value, such as moving down by one centimetre. In Figure 11d, fixed size threshold filters out small watch. The fix is to derive the value from the state. 5.3. The Upper Bound of COAP Finding 6. The upper bound of COAP is set by two factors: how accurately and comprehensively the program represents the state, and how robust the code logic is, for example whether it is aware of failures and retries. State representation. Perception and contact errors, 62% of failures, are limits of state measurement (Figure 11, left). Perception errors arise because the input is RGB only, so some estimates are inaccurate. Contact errors arise because the physical state is hard to represent: for deformable or otherwise complex objects, part of the contact is not represented well. The more accurately the state is represented, the higher the upper bound of COAP. Robust code logic. Incomplete logic and poor code design, 37% of failures, are limits of the logic (Figure 11, right). More robust code removes them: functions that notice their own failures, retry with another method, and derive values from the state. 5.4. Limitations Simulation only. All results are currently in simulation. COAPs perception relies on the public configuration and assets of the simulated benchmark, such as the camera parameters, the robot meshes, and the object sizes, which is major limitation. On real robot, these would have to be measured, and contact-related parameters, such as grip widths and carry speeds, tuned again. Offline development. Online execution is fast, but offline development takes time: each iteration of the code needs evaluation and revision. Unlike model such as GPT, which can be used directly as policy, COAP has development cost for every new task. Figure 11. Four classes of error. Each column gives the share of failures in one class, two frames of one failed episode from the official video, and the fix. 17 Generalization. Code may have limited generalization capabilities. In principle, the upper bound of code is high, and it rises as the state is represented more clearly (5.3), but COAP currently succeeds only in 70.24% of episodes. Part of the gap comes from incomplete logic and poor code design (5.2), such as hard-coded value that works only in the cases it was written for. In addition, the programs were developed on validation layouts and never on the test layouts, so lower success on layouts the code has not seen is to be expected, especially on the randomized layouts of the Generalization tasks, with new objects, rooms, and distractors (54.1%, against 77.3% on their standard layouts). Still, the code does not depend on the scene: each program is task-level code, the library is shared across tasks, and on standard layouts, success on test layouts (74.9%) stays close to that on validation layouts (76.7%). Although code has such limits, in scenes where the state is clear, it runs stably and can produce data reliably (5.5). 5.5. COAP as an efficient Data Engine for VLAs, Agent-as-Policy and Harness VLA Finding 8. COAP produces successful trajectories quickly and reproducibly, so it can serve as data engine for VLAs, Agent-as-Policy, and Harness VLA. Once task program works, it runs on CPU without model and can be executed on many layouts in parallel, so successful trajectories can be obtained very quickly. Each trajectory comes with the programs explicit state and the decision behind every action, because the policy is white box. These trajectories can train VLA, and the recorded states and decisions can supervise the model inside an Agent Harness. COAP can therefore benefit the development of VLAs and Agent Harnesses. new direction. Code-Only-as-Policy differs in many ways from VLAs, World Action Models, and Agent Harnesses (Agent-as-Policy and Harness VLA, which keep model in the control loop): its state is explicit, no model runs during execution, and the policy is improved by coding agents rather than by training on data. Since its approach differs in so many ways, we view it as new direction. If the embodied world is Turing machine, code can be universal interface to the physical world (1). Our analysis suggests that this direction has advantages (4.34.4), and we hope that our exploration can benefit VLAs, Agent-as-Policy, Harness VLA, and RSI. 6. Conclusion We propose that the embodied world, robot together with its environment, is in essence an Embodied Turing Machine: the world state is its tape, and the robot policy is its rules. On this basis, we introduce Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP), whose approach differs from those of existing directions, such as VLAs, World Action Models, and Agent-as-Policy: the state is explicit, the rules are code, and coding agents improve the code. On RoboDojo, COAP succeeds in 70.24% of episodes, 38.9% above the state-of-the-art method, and leads all five dimensions. Compared with VLA and an Agent Harness, COAP has three advantages (4.3): Explicit State, Execution, and Extensibility. Because the policy is white box, it suits RSI, and its development is efficient (4.4). Code still has an upper bound, set by the state representation and the code logic (5.2 5.3), but as coding agents become stronger, this upper bound will rise. We also believe that COAP can serve as an efficient data engine for VLAs, Agent-as-Policy, and Harness VLA (5.5).

With the tasks whose code was later cleaned up included, success went from 80.0% to 81.4%. The test detects pooled shift of about 4 points, so it rules out large regression, not every change. 25 Extension without breaking. Figure 14 shows how new tasks extend the library. new task adds its own files and changes no line of an existing one (a). New behaviour reaches other tasks by call to an existing library function, by inheritance, or by parameter that is off by default, so every other caller runs the same code path as before (Eq. 3) and only the tasks that pass the new parameter change (b). sweep_blocks, for example, reuses the sliding function added to the library for push_T (c). Parallel Branching: Details Branches and the estimate. branch is variant of program that changes one decision and is evaluated on the same seeds and layouts as its parent. Figure 10b uses every branch whose validation success was measured against its immediate parent. Repeated runs of the same program differ by one to three episodes per evaluation, so the selection margin of four episodes is one to two noise widths. The estimate of Figure 10c draws 𝑘 effects with replacement from the measured ones and keeps the best if it reaches the margin, otherwise the parent; the bands are the 5th and 95th percentiles over bootstrap resamples. The estimate treats branches of one decision as independent and pools effects across tasks, and each gain is measured on the layouts that selected it, so the true gain is somewhat lower. 26 All tasks at once. and finished in 17% of the time they would have taken one after another. In the busiest window of development, evaluations of 12 tasks ran in parallel Merges and test. After the library was frozen, task updates were merged one at time, each changing shared code only through default-off parameters, and overall success rose at every merge, from 66.5% to 70.24%. Changes are selected on validation, and the gains carry over to test: on the 40 tasks with program, standard success is 76.7% on validation and 74.9% on test, and randomized success 55.2% and 52.8%.
